n: Some months after Ezra’s arrival, local leaders report a serious problem: many Israelites, even priests and Levites, have adopted the ways of surrounding peoples. The list echoes the nations Moses warned Israel about centuries before.

f.g: The concern was not ethnicity but religion — adopting the idol worship and practices of these peoples.

f.w: the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites

n: The specific sin is marrying outside the covenant, which had led Israel into idolatry before. Worse, the leaders were the first offenders.

f.g: Israel as a people set apart for God by covenant (compare Isaiah 6:13).

n: Ezra is crushed. Tearing his clothes and pulling out his hair were ancient signs of overwhelming grief and horror.

f.g: Tore my clothing — a customary act of mourning.

n: Those who took God’s word seriously gather around Ezra. He sits in silent mourning all afternoon until the evening sacrifice, around 3 p.m.

f.w: trembled at the words of the God of Israel

f.g: The daily afternoon offering at the temple (Exodus 29:38-41).

n: At the hour of prayer, Ezra kneels and spreads out his hands toward heaven — a posture of pleading. His prayer follows.
Ezra’s prayer begins with shame. Notice he says “our” iniquities — though he was not guilty himself, he stands with his people and confesses as one of them.
He reviews Israel’s history: centuries of disobedience led to conquest and exile. The scattering of Israel was the direct result of breaking covenants.

f.w: delivered into the hand of the kings of the lands

n: Yet God showed grace for “a little space,” preserving a remnant. A “nail” was a tent peg — a small but firm hold in God’s holy place, a fresh start.

f.w: a nail in his holy place
f.g: A tent peg — a secure foothold; compare Isaiah 22:23.
To brighten our eyes — renew life and hope.

n: Even while under Persian rule, God moved kings to let them rebuild the temple. The “wall” here likely means God’s protection rather than literal city walls, which Nehemiah would build later.

f.g: Probably a figure for safety and protection; Jerusalem’s actual walls were rebuilt under Nehemiah.

f.w: in the sight of the kings of Persia

n: After such kindness, Ezra has no excuse to offer. The honest response to God’s mercy is confession, not self-justification.
Ezra summarizes the warnings of Moses and the prophets: the land was polluted by the corrupt practices of its earlier peoples.

The command was not to intermarry with these peoples, so Israel could stay strong and pass on the land and the covenant to its children. Marriage within the covenant protects the faith of future generations.

f.w: give not your daughters unto their sons
leave it for an inheritance to your children

n: Ezra acknowledges that God punished them less than they deserved. Recognizing God’s mercy is a key step in true repentance.

f.w: punished us less than our iniquities deserve

n: Having been rescued once, should they now repeat the same sin? Ezra fears that continued rebellion would bring complete destruction.
Ezra ends not by asking for anything, but by admitting God is righteous and they are guilty. He simply places the people, with their sins, before the Lord.
